title: 01. Fundamentals: String Methods — Search & Find
summary: Search methods help you find characters or substrings within a string. These are among the most used string methods in real applications.

sections.title: CONCEPT EXPLANATION
sections.body:
Search methods help you **find characters or substrings** within a string. These are among the most used string methods in real applications.

### Complete Search Methods:

| Method | Returns | If Not Found |
|---|---|---|
| `.find(sub)` | Index of FIRST occurrence | `-1` |
| `.rfind(sub)` | Index of LAST occurrence | `-1` |
| `.index(sub)` | Index of FIRST occurrence | `ValueError` |
| `.rindex(sub)` | Index of LAST occurrence | `ValueError` |
| `.count(sub)` | Number of occurrences | `0` |
| `.startswith(prefix)` | `True`/`False` | — |
| `.endswith(suffix)` | `True`/`False` | — |

### `find()` vs `index()` — Critical Difference:
```python
text = "Hello World"

# find() — SAFE: returns -1 if not found
print(text.find("xyz"))    # -1  ← no crash

# index() — UNSAFE: raises ValueError if not found
try:
    text.index("xyz")      # ValueError!
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")   # substring not found
```

### ⚠️ Use Cases:
- `find()` → When the substring might not be there (safe)
- `index()` → When it MUST be there (fail loudly if missing)

sections.title: 5 EXAMPLES
sections.body:
### Example 1: `find()` and `rfind()` — Finding Positions
```python
text = "Python is great. Python is powerful. Python rocks!"

# find() — returns index of FIRST occurrence
pos = text.find("Python")
print(f"First 'Python' at index: {pos}")   # 0

# find() with start position
pos2 = text.find("Python", 1)     # Search from index 1
print(f"Next 'Python' after 0: {pos2}")    # 17

# find() with start and end
pos3 = text.find("Python", 1, 25)  # Search only in [1:25]
print(f"'Python' in [1:25]: {pos3}")  # 17 (if found) or -1

# rfind() — LAST occurrence
last = text.rfind("Python")
print(f"Last 'Python' at index: {last}")   # 37

# find() returns -1 if not found — safe to use in conditions!
pos4 = text.find("Java")
print(f"'Java' found at: {pos4}")   # -1
if pos4 != -1:
    print("Java found!")
else:
    print("Java not found ✅")

# Find ALL occurrences using a loop
def find_all(text, sub):
    positions = []
    start = 0
    while True:
        pos = text.find(sub, start)
        if pos == -1:
            break
        positions.append(pos)
        start = pos + 1
    return positions

print(f"All 'Python' positions: {find_all(text, 'Python')}")
# [0, 17, 37]
```

### Example 2: `count()` — Count Occurrences
```python
text = "banana"

print(text.count("a"))         # 3
print(text.count("an"))        # 2
print(text.count("ana"))       # 1 (non-overlapping!)
print(text.count("x"))         # 0

# Non-overlapping explanation:
text2 = "aaa"
print(text2.count("aa"))       # 1 — not 2! (non-overlapping)
# Finds "aa" at index 0, then searches from index 2 — only 'a' left

# Practical: count words in text
sentence = "to be or not to be that is the question"
print(f"'to' appears: {sentence.count('to ')} times")   # 2

# Count specific characters
code = "def my_function(x, y, z):\n    return x + y + z"
print(f"Lines: {code.count(chr(10)) + 1}")       # Count \n + 1
print(f"Parameters: {code.count(',') + 1}")       # Count commas + 1 (approx)
print(f"Spaces: {code.count(' ')}")

# Word frequency (simplified version)
words = "the cat sat on the mat the cat is fat".split()
unique = set(words)
freq   = {word: words.count(word) for word in unique}
sorted_freq = sorted(freq.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
print("\nWord frequencies:", sorted_freq[:5])
```

### Example 3: `startswith()` and `endswith()` — Prefix/Suffix Checking
```python
# Basic usage
filename = "report_2026.pdf"
print(filename.endswith(".pdf"))      # True
print(filename.endswith(".csv"))      # False
print(filename.startswith("report"))  # True
print(filename.startswith("daily"))   # False

# Multiple options — pass a TUPLE (not list!)
def categorize_file(filename):
    filename = filename.lower()
    if filename.endswith((".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".gif", ".webp")):
        return "image"
    elif filename.endswith((".mp4", ".avi", ".mov", ".mkv")):
        return "video"
    elif filename.endswith((".pdf", ".doc", ".docx", ".txt")):
        return "document"
    elif filename.endswith((".py", ".js", ".java", ".cpp", ".ts")):
        return "code"
    else:
        return "unknown"

files = ["photo.JPG", "video.mp4", "report.PDF", "app.py",
         "data.xlsx", "music.mp3"]
for f in files:
    print(f"  {f:<20}: {categorize_file(f)}")

# startswith with tuple — check multiple prefixes
urls = [
    "https://secure.example.com",
    "http://old.example.com",
    "ftp://files.example.com",
    "mailto:user@example.com",
]
for url in urls:
    is_web = url.startswith(("http://", "https://"))
    print(f"  {url[:30]}: {'🌐 Web' if is_web else '📁 Other'}")
```

### Example 4: `index()` and `rindex()` — When Key Must Exist
```python
# Use index() when the character MUST be there
# (fail loudly if something is wrong with your data)

def parse_email(email):
    """Parse email — will raise ValueError if format is wrong"""
    try:
        at_pos     = email.index("@")           # MUST have @
        dot_pos    = email.rindex(".", at_pos)  # MUST have . after @

        username   = email[:at_pos]
        domain     = email[at_pos+1:dot_pos]
        extension  = email[dot_pos+1:]

        return {"username": username, "domain": domain, "ext": extension}

    except ValueError as e:
        return {"error": f"Invalid email format: {e}"}

emails = [
    "veerababu@example.com",
    "alice@company.co.uk",
    "invalid-email",
    "no-at-sign.com",
]

for email in emails:
    result = parse_email(email)
    print(f"  {email:<30}: {result}")

# rindex() — last occurrence (useful for file paths)
path = "/home/user/documents/projects/report.pdf"
last_slash = path.rindex("/")
filename   = path[last_slash+1:]
directory  = path[:last_slash]
print(f"\nFile: {filename}")    # report.pdf
print(f"Dir:  {directory}")    # /home/user/documents/projects
```

### Example 5: Search Methods for Data Validation
```python
def validate_and_parse_connection_string(conn_str):
    """
    Parse: "postgresql://user:password@host:5432/dbname"
    Use find/index/startswith for robust parsing
    """
    result = {"valid": False, "errors": []}

    # Check protocol
    if not conn_str.startswith(("postgresql://", "mysql://", "sqlite://")):
        result["errors"].append("Unknown protocol")
        return result

    # Find protocol
    protocol_end = conn_str.index("://")
    result["protocol"] = conn_str[:protocol_end]

    rest = conn_str[protocol_end + 3:]  # After "://"

    # Find credentials (before @)
    at_pos = rest.find("@")
    if at_pos != -1:
        credentials = rest[:at_pos]
        rest = rest[at_pos+1:]

        colon_pos = credentials.find(":")
        if colon_pos != -1:
            result["user"]     = credentials[:colon_pos]
            result["password"] = credentials[colon_pos+1:]
        else:
            result["user"] = credentials

    # Find host:port/dbname
    slash_pos = rest.find("/")
    if slash_pos != -1:
        host_port     = rest[:slash_pos]
        result["db"]  = rest[slash_pos+1:]
    else:
        host_port = rest

    colon_pos = host_port.find(":")
    if colon_pos != -1:
        result["host"] = host_port[:colon_pos]
        result["port"] = int(host_port[colon_pos+1:])
    else:
        result["host"] = host_port

    result["valid"] = True
    return result

conn = "postgresql://admin:secret@db.server.com:5432/myapp"
parsed = validate_and_parse_connection_string(conn)
for k, v in parsed.items():
    print(f"  {k:<10}: {v}")
```
